claims.text: A controlled, non-uniform distribution of Al, Cr, or Mn prior to oxidation promotes rapid nucleation and uniform growth of a continuous passivating oxide scale.
The passivating scale produced by engineered elemental partitioning is adherent.
Engineered elemental partitioning enhances oxidation resistance and prolongs material integrity during sustained high-temperature exposure.
A typical as-cast or conventionally heat-treated MPEA has a homogeneous, balanced distribution of oxide-forming and non-oxide-forming elements.
Tailored heat treatment can induce local enrichment or partitioning of Al, Cr, and Mn in an MPEA.
Spatially enriched regions of oxide-forming elements provide controlled nucleation sites for protective oxide phases.
Al and Cr can form passivating Al2O3 and Cr2O3 in AlCoCrFeNi alloys.
A dense MnCr2O4/Al2O3 duplex scale can be thin, continuous, and protective after oxidation at 900°C for 120 hours.
Localized enrichment of oxide-forming elements accelerates formation of a thin, continuous oxide scale by localizing passivating-phase nucleation.
A continuous protective scale suppresses oxygen ingress and outward metal-cation diffusion.
Suppressing oxygen ingress and cation diffusion reduces overall oxide-scale thickness.
Localized enrichment of oxide-forming elements reduces the likelihood of scale spallation.
Relative to a homogeneous baseline, the engineered alloy will develop a thinner, more compositionally uniform, less porous, and more adherent oxide scale.
The governing behavior should hold from approximately 800°C to 1100°C under controlled oxidizing atmospheres.
The governing behavior should persist for prolonged exposures around 120 hours.
Reactive-element additions such as Y can independently improve scale-alloy bonding and prevent spallation.
Hf may confound the effect attributed to engineered elemental partitioning.
Processing differences such as conventional casting versus laser cladding can independently affect oxidation resistance through grain refinement and accelerated Al and Cr transport.
Oxide chemistry and structure in equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn evolve over time according to element-environment interactions, with redox potential becoming dominant at later stages.
If the engineered samples are statistically indistinguishable from or worse than the baseline in scale thickness, adherence, and compositional uniformity, the hypothesis is falsified.
